# Part 1 · Identifiers

Every merge needs a **key**: one or more variables that identify an observation uniquely. In accounting research, the most important keys are:

| Identifier | Identifies | Source | Watch out |
|------------|------------|--------|-----------|
| `gvkey` | a firm | Compustat | 6-digit **text** with leading zeros |
| `permno` | a security (share class) | CRSP | a firm can have several permnos |
| `cusip` | a security | US/Canada | changes after name changes |
| `ticker` | a security | exchanges | **reused** after delistings |
| `isin` | a security | international | 12 characters, starts with a country code |
| company name | — | everywhere | spelling varies: "BMW" vs. "Bayerische Motoren Werke AG" |

A key for **firm-year data** is usually a combination, e.g. `gvkey` + `fyear`.

### Chunk 1.1 · Why names are bad keys

```{r chunk_1_1}
## Join by name: how many matches?

## Two small "databases" with the same 3 firms, names written differently (illustrative numbers)
db_a <- tibble(
  name  = c("BMW", "Siemens AG", "SAP"),
  isin  = c("DE0005190003", "DE0007236101", "DE0007164600"),
  sales = c(155, 78, 31)
)
db_b <- tibble(
  name   = c("Bayerische Motoren Werke AG", "Siemens", "SAP SE"),
  isin   = c("DE0005190003", "DE0007236101", "DE0007164600"),
  assets = c(255, 145, 74)
)

## Join by name: keep only rows whose names match exactly
by_name <- inner_join(db_a, db_b, by = "name")
nrow(by_name)            # 0 - not a single match!

## Join by ISIN: a real identifier
by_isin <- inner_join(db_a, db_b, by = "isin")
by_isin
nrow(by_isin)            # 3 - all firms match

```

*Illustrative numbers.* Not a single match — although all three firms are in both tables. That is why we use codes such as `isin` or `gvkey`, and why name matching ("fuzzy matching") is a last resort that must be checked by hand.

### Chunk 1.2 · What does a valid ISIN look like?

An ISIN has 12 characters: a 2-letter country code, 9 alphanumeric characters and a check digit, e.g. `DE0005190003` (BMW).

```{r chunk_1_2}
## Repair what can be repaired: trim spaces, upper case

## Some ISINs as they might come from a messy source
isins <- c("DE0005190003",     # valid (BMW)
           " DE0007236101 ",   # spaces around it
           "de0007164600",     # lower case
           "DE000519000",      # only 11 characters - something is missing
           "BMW")              # a name, not an ISIN

## Rule for a valid ISIN: 2 capital letters + 9 letters/digits + 1 digit = 12 characters
isin_pattern <- "^[A-Z]{2}[A-Z0-9]{9}[0-9]$"

## Before repair: which entries are valid?
str_detect(isins, isin_pattern)       # TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

## Repair: remove spaces at the edges, make letters capital
isins_clean <- isins |>
  str_trim() |>
  str_to_upper()
isins_clean

## After repair: 3 valid, the last 2 cannot be repaired (missing digit, not an ISIN)
str_detect(isins_clean, isin_pattern) # TRUE TRUE TRUE FALSE FALSE

```

**Lesson:** before you merge, check that keys look the way they should. A lower-case letter or an invisible space is enough to break a merge — without any error message.

# Part 2 · Getting data from an API: the SRN database

The **Sustainability Reporting Navigator (SRN)** collects data from European sustainability reports (ESRS). Its *Main ESRS KPI* dataset contains 27 indicators (emissions, energy, employees, revenues, …) for more than 600 firms, partly extracted by humans and partly by AI.

An **API** (application programming interface) lets your code ask a server for data:

1.  You send a **request** to a URL (an *endpoint*), often with a **token** that says who you are.
2.  The server sends a **response**: a status code (200 = OK, 401 = not authorised, 404 = not found) and the data, usually as JSON or CSV.

Advantages over clicking "download": the download becomes part of your code, so it is **documented and reproducible** — and you can pin an exact version of the data.

### Chunk 2.1 · An open endpoint: release metadata (no token needed)

```{r api_2_1}
## Release list of the Main ESRS KPI dataset
resp_rel <- request("https://api.srnav.com") |>
  req_url_path_append("projects", "main-esrs-kpi", "releases") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("SRN_TOKEN")) |>   # token from .Renviron, never in the code
  req_perform()
resp_status(resp_rel)          # 200 = OK

## Save a raw copy: raw data is never edited
writeBin(resp_body_raw(resp_rel), here("data", "srn_releases.json"))
```

```{r chunk_2_1b}
## Read the saved raw copy and look at it
releases <- jsonlite::fromJSON(here("data", "srn_releases.json"))
str(releases)       # what's inside?
releases
```

### Chunk 2.2 · Your API token: keep it secret

The data values need a personal token. Create one at **srnav.com → MySRN → API** (`srnav.com/dashboard/api`).

**Never** write the token into your R Markdown — it would end up on GitHub. Store it in your personal `.Renviron` file instead:

```{r chunk_2_2, eval=FALSE}
## Run ONCE in the Console. A file opens: add the line
##   SRN_TOKEN=srn_your_token_here
## save it, then restart R (Session -> Restart R).
usethis::edit_r_environ()

## Check (shows TRUE, not the token itself)
nchar(Sys.getenv("SRN_TOKEN")) > 0
```

### Chunk 2.3 · Download the data values (pinned to release v2.4)

```{r api_2_3}
## Download release v2.4 (pinned: always the same data, not "latest")
resp <- request("https://api.srnav.com") |>
  req_url_path_append("projects", "main-esrs-kpi", "releases", "v2.4.csv") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("SRN_TOKEN")) |>
  req_perform()
resp_status(resp)              # 200 = OK, 401 = token wrong

## Save the raw download unchanged
writeBin(resp_body_raw(resp), here("data", "srn_main_esrs_kpi_v2.4.csv"))
```

**Why `v2.4` and not `latest`?** `latest` changes whenever SRN publishes a new release. Your results would change without you noticing. Pinning the version makes your analysis reproducible.

### Chunk 2.4 · Read and inspect the raw data

```{r chunk_2_4}
## Read the saved raw copy (not the server again)
srn_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "srn_main_esrs_kpi_v2.4.csv"))
glimpse(srn_raw)                       # columns and their types

## One row per ... ?
srn_raw |> count(company_id, year, field_slug) |> filter(n > 1)   # empty = one row per company × year × indicator

## The value column: numbers as text — and a special code
class(srn_raw$value)                   # "character", not numeric!
srn_raw |>
  filter(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value)))) |>   # values that are NOT a number
  count(value, sort = TRUE)            # which texts appear, and how often?
```

The data are in **long format**: one row per company × year × indicator. For analysis we usually want **wide format**: one row per company-year, one column per indicator (Chunk 3.4).

# Part 3 · Missing values and duplicates

## Missing values

A missing value (`NA`) can mean very different things:

-   the firm **did not report** the indicator (e.g. no Scope 3 emissions),
-   the indicator **does not apply** (e.g. no land use for a software firm),
-   the value **was not extracted** (yet) — a data problem, not a firm decision.

These are different economic stories. Treating all of them as "zero" or simply dropping them can bias your results.

### Chunk 3.1 · How much is missing?

```{r chunk_3_1}
## Missing per variable
colSums(is.na(srn_raw))                          # number of NAs in each column

## Three kinds of "missing" in the SRN data:
##   (1) value is NA, (2) value is the code "NOT_FOUND", (3) the row does not exist at all
sum(is.na(srn_raw$value))                        # (1) NA
sum(srn_raw$value == "NOT_FOUND", na.rm = TRUE)  # (2) special code

## (3) Missing rows: how many company-years should there be?
n_company_years <- srn_raw |> distinct(company_id, year) |> nrow()
n_fields        <- n_distinct(srn_raw$field_slug)     # number of indicators (should be 27)
n_company_years * n_fields                       # rows if every indicator existed for every company-year
nrow(srn_raw)                                    # rows that actually exist
n_company_years * n_fields - nrow(srn_raw)       # (3) rows that are missing entirely
```

### Chunk 3.2 · Text that looks fine but is not

```{r chunk_3_2}
isin_pattern <- "^[A-Z]{2}[A-Z0-9]{9}[0-9]$"   # valid ISIN: 2 letters + 9 letters/digits + 1 digit

## Countries: spot the problem
srn_firms <- srn_raw |> distinct(company_id, country, isin)   # one row per firm
srn_firms |> count(country, sort = TRUE)          # look for "the same" country twice

## Invisible trailing spaces
srn_firms |>
  filter(country != str_trim(country)) |>         # text changes when spaces are trimmed
  distinct(country)                               # e.g. "Austria " (with a space)

## Firms without ISIN: what do their IDs look like?
srn_firms |>
  filter(is.na(isin) | !str_detect(isin, isin_pattern)) |>    # missing or not a valid ISIN
  head(10)

## Does the ISIN country prefix match the country? (not always — and that can be fine)
srn_firms |>
  mutate(prefix = str_sub(isin, 1, 2)) |>         # first 2 characters, e.g. "DE"
  count(country, prefix, sort = TRUE)
```

## Duplicates

Before you merge or reshape, check that your key is unique: **one row per key**. If not, find out *why* before you decide what to do.

### Chunk 3.3 · Is the key unique?

```{r chunk_3_3}
## SRN: key = company_id + year + field_slug
srn_raw |> count(company_id, year, field_slug) |> filter(n > 1)   # 0 rows = unique

## Compustat (Tutorial 1): key = gvkey + fyear?
cs <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"),
               col_types = cols(gvkey = "c"), guess_max = Inf)   # safe import from Tutorial 1
dups <- cs |> count(gvkey, fyear) |> filter(n > 1)
nrow(dups)                       # how many firm-years appear more than once?
head(dups)

## Why? Look at one duplicate
cs |>
  filter(gvkey == "001062", fyear == 2010) |>         # example from the slide
  select(gvkey, fyear, datadate, indfmt, at, sale)    # which column differs?
```

The Compustat duplicates are the same firm-year in two **formats**: `INDL` (industrial) and `FS` (financial services). The standard solution is to keep `indfmt == "INDL"`.

```{r chunk_3_3b}
## Keep the industrial format only
cs_indl <- cs |> filter(indfmt == "INDL")

## Who is left?
nrow(cs)                                         # before
nrow(cs_indl)                                    # after: fewer rows
cs_indl |> count(gvkey, fyear) |> filter(n > 1)  # key now unique? (0 rows = yes)
```

One firm reports **two fiscal year-ends per year** — it changed its fiscal year (June → December) and Compustat keeps both. A rule we can defend: keep the later `datadate` per firm-year.

```{r chunk_3_3c}
## Which firm-year still has two rows? (the fiscal year change)
cs_indl |> count(gvkey, fyear) |> filter(n > 1)

## Rule: keep the later datadate per firm-year
cs_clean <- cs_indl |>
  group_by(gvkey, fyear) |>
  slice_max(datadate, n = 1) |>      # keep the row with the latest datadate in each group
  ungroup()

## Check: key unique now? (0 rows = yes)
cs_clean |> count(gvkey, fyear) |> filter(n > 1)
nrow(cs_indl) - nrow(cs_clean)       # how many rows were dropped
```

### Chunk 3.4 · From long to wide

```{r chunk_3_4}
## Values are text. Convert the numeric indicators:
srn_num <- srn_raw |>
  mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value)))   # "NOT_FOUND" and other text -> NA

## How many values could not be converted? (should match the special codes from Chunk 3.1)
sum(is.na(srn_num$value_num) & !is.na(srn_num$value))

## Long -> wide: one row per company × year, one column per indicator
srn_wide <- srn_num |>
  select(company_id, year, field_slug, value_num) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = field_slug, values_from = value_num)

dim(srn_wide)          # rows = company-years, columns = 2 keys + 27 indicators
head(srn_wide)
```

**Task A:** Which share of firm-years reports Scope 1, Scope 2 (market-based) and Scope 3 emissions? Is "missing" here a firm decision or a data problem? How would you find out?

```{r task_A}
## Share of firm-years reporting each emission scope
srn_wide |>
  summarise(
    scope1     = mean(!is.na(ghg_scope1)),
    scope2_mkt = mean(!is.na(ghg_scope2_mkt)),
    scope3     = mean(!is.na(ghg_scope3))
  )

## Is "missing" a firm decision or a data problem? Look at the raw codes:
srn_raw |>
  filter(field_slug %in% c("ghg_scope1", "ghg_scope2_mkt", "ghg_scope3")) |>
  mutate(kind = case_when(is.na(value)         ~ "NA (not extracted?)",
                          value == "NOT_FOUND" ~ "NOT_FOUND (not reported?)",
                          TRUE                 ~ "number")) |>
  count(field_slug, kind)
```

# Part 4 · Merges: rebuilding a Ball & Brown (1968) sample

Ball and Brown (1968) needed **three data sources**: annual earnings (Compustat), monthly stock returns (CRSP) and announcement dates (Wall Street Journal). Their inclusion criteria (p. 167):

1.  earnings data available on Compustat for each of the years 1946–1966,
2.  fiscal year ending December 31,
3.  price data available on CRSP for at least 100 months,
4.  Wall Street Journal announcement dates available.

Result: **261 firms**. Today we build a modern version for 2010–2014 and count, step by step, how many firms survive each criterion (a **sample funnel**).

## Joins in dplyr

| Function | Keeps |
|----------|-------|
| `left_join(x, y)` | all rows of `x`; `NA` where `y` has no match |
| `inner_join(x, y)` | only rows with a match in both |
| `anti_join(x, y)` | rows of `x` **without** a match in `y` — your best diagnostic tool |
| `full_join(x, y)` | all rows of both |

**Fan-out:** if a key appears twice in `y`, every matching row in `x` is duplicated. Always compare the number of rows before and after a join.

### Chunk 4.1 · Step 1: Compustat — US firms, earnings available, December year-end

A small helper records firms and firm-years after every step (given — just run it):

```{r funnel_helper}
funnel <- tibble(step = character(), firms = integer(), firm_years = integer())
add_step <- function(funnel, step, data) {
  add_row(funnel, step = step, firms = n_distinct(data$gvkey), firm_years = nrow(data))
}
```

```{r chunk_4_1}
## Step 0: Compustat INDL, one row per firm-year, fiscal year known
bb <- cs_clean |> filter(!is.na(fyear))
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "Compustat INDL, fiscal year known", bb)

## Step 1: US firms reporting in USD
bb <- bb |> filter(fic == "USA", curcd == "USD")
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "US firms reporting in USD", bb)

## Step 2: earnings (ib = income before extraordinary items) available
bb <- bb |> filter(!is.na(ib))
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "Earnings (ib) available", bb)

## Step 3: fiscal year ends in December
bb <- bb |> filter(month(datadate) == 12)
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "Fiscal year ends in December", bb)

funnel        # compare with the slide: 14,662 / 10,424 / 7,878 / 5,980 firms
```

### Chunk 4.2 · Step 2: the CRSP–Compustat link table

Compustat identifies **firms** (`gvkey`), CRSP identifies **securities** (`permno`). The link table says which permno belongs to which gvkey — and **when** (`linkdt` to `linkenddt`).

```{r chunk_4_2}
## Read the link table: all columns as text first (keeps gvkey's leading zeros)
link <- read_csv(here("data", "crsp_ccm_link.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = "c")) |>
  rename_with(tolower)                       # LINKTYPE -> linktype etc.

## Standard filters (slide): reliable links, primary security
link <- link |>
  filter(linktype %in% c("LU", "LC"),
         linkprim %in% c("P", "C")) |>
  mutate(permno    = as.integer(lpermno),
         linkdt    = as.Date(linkdt),
         linkenddt = as.Date(if_else(is.na(linkenddt) | linkenddt == "E",
                                     as.character(Sys.Date()), linkenddt)))   # open link -> today

## Look at it
head(link)
link |> count(gvkey) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()   # firms with more than one link over time
```

Standard choice: keep primary links (`linkprim` P or C) of the reliable types `LU` and `LC`. An open-ended link has no end date (`E` or missing) — we set it to "today".

```{r chunk_4_2b}
## How many permnos per gvkey (over all time)?
link |>
  group_by(gvkey) |>
  summarise(n_permno = n_distinct(permno)) |>   # number of different permnos per firm
  count(n_permno)                               # how many firms have 1, 2, 3, ... permnos
```

### Chunk 4.3 · Merge with a date condition

A plain join by `gvkey` attaches **every** link ever valid for that firm → fan-out. We must keep only the link valid on the fiscal year-end date (`datadate`).

```{r chunk_4_3}
## Naive join: what happens to the number of rows?
bb_naive <- bb |> inner_join(link, by = "gvkey", relationship = "many-to-many")
nrow(bb)                 # before
nrow(bb_naive)           # after: more rows = fan-out!

## Correct: keep only links valid on datadate
bb_linked <- bb |>
  inner_join(link, by = join_by(gvkey, between(datadate, linkdt, linkenddt)))
nrow(bb_linked)

## Check the key again: one row per gvkey-fyear?
bb_linked |> count(gvkey, fyear) |> filter(n > 1)    # 0 rows = yes

## Who got lost? anti_join shows firms without a valid link
lost <- bb |> anti_join(bb_linked, by = c("gvkey", "fyear"))
nrow(lost)               # firm-years without a CRSP link
head(lost)

## Add to the funnel
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "Valid CRSP link at fiscal year-end", bb_linked)
funnel
```

### Chunk 4.4 · Step 3: CRSP returns — at least 60 months of returns

Ball and Brown required 100 months of price data. Our CRSP extract covers 2009–2015 (84 months), so we require **60 months**.

```{r chunk_4_4}
## Read the CRSP monthly stock file
msf <- read_csv(here("data", "crsp_msf_2009_2015.csv")) |>
  rename_with(tolower)                     # PERMNO -> permno, MthRet -> mthret, ...

## Key check: one row per permno and month?
msf_dups <- msf |> count(permno, mthcaldt) |> filter(n > 1)
nrow(msf_dups)                             # number of permno-months that appear more than once

## Look at one duplicate: are the rows identical?
first_dup <- msf_dups |> slice(1)
msf |> semi_join(first_dup, by = c("permno", "mthcaldt"))   # show all rows of that permno-month
```

Most of these duplicates are **exact copies** of the same row; in the others only the ticker differs (the firm changed its ticker that month). Return and price are identical, so we can keep one row — but only after we checked that they really are identical.

```{r chunk_4_4b}
## Tickers are not stable: one permno, several tickers
msf |>
  group_by(permno) |>
  summarise(n_tickers = n_distinct(ticker)) |>
  count(n_tickers)                         # how many permnos had 1, 2, 3, ... tickers

## Check before removing: within each duplicate, are return and price identical?
msf |>
  group_by(permno, mthcaldt) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>                       # only duplicated permno-months
  summarise(n_ret = n_distinct(mthret), n_prc = n_distinct(mthprc), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_ret > 1 | n_prc > 1)            # 0 rows = return and price always identical

## Safe to keep one row per permno-month
msf_clean <- msf |> distinct(permno, mthcaldt, .keep_all = TRUE)
msf_clean |> count(permno, mthcaldt) |> filter(n > 1)   # 0 rows = key unique now
```

**Task B:** Look at the funnel. Which criterion removes the most firms? Which kinds of firms are lost (think: young firms, failed firms, foreign firms)? Ball and Brown wrote that their sample "does not include young firms, those which have failed …". What does that mean for the results?
Answer B: "US firms reporting in USD" removes the most firms. Lost are foreign firms, firms with
other year-ends, and young or delisted firms. Like Ball and Brown, the sample only keeps survivors
(survivorship bias), so the results may not hold for young or failing firms.

```{r task_B}
## Last funnel step: at least 60 monthly returns on CRSP
permnos_60 <- msf_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(mthret)) |>
  count(permno) |>                          # number of months with a return per permno
  filter(n >= 60)

bb_final <- bb_linked |> semi_join(permnos_60, by = "permno")
funnel <- add_step(funnel, "At least 60 monthly returns on CRSP", bb_final)

## The funnel, with the number of firms lost in each step
funnel |> mutate(firms_lost = lag(firms) - firms)
```


### Chunk 4.5 · Bonus: the Ball & Brown idea in five lines

Do firms with **earnings increases** have higher stock returns over the fiscal year than firms with earnings decreases?

```{r chunk_4_5}
## Good news = earnings (ib) higher than last year
bb_news <- bb_final |>
  arrange(gvkey, fyear) |>
  group_by(gvkey) |>
  mutate(good_news = ib > lag(ib)) |>          # TRUE = increase, FALSE = decrease
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(good_news)) |>                 # first year has no previous year
  mutate(start = datadate %m-% months(12))     # fiscal year = 12 months up to datadate

## Annual return: compound the 12 monthly returns of the fiscal year
bb_ret <- bb_news |>
  inner_join(msf_clean, by = join_by(permno, start < mthcaldt, datadate >= mthcaldt)) |>
  group_by(gvkey, fyear, good_news) |>
  summarise(ret = prod(1 + mthret, na.rm = TRUE) - 1, .groups = "drop")

## The Ball & Brown comparison: average return, good vs. bad news
bb_ret |> group_by(good_news) |> summarise(mean_ret = mean(ret), n = n())
```

# Part 5 · Auditing extracted data: SRN vs. Compustat

SRN values are extracted from sustainability reports — partly by humans, partly by AI. SRN's own quality snapshot reports that about **74%** of the reviewed values are correct. Blankespoor, Croom and Grant (2026) classify investor questions with a machine-learning model that agrees with human coders in about **75%** of cases. In both cases: generated data are useful, but they must be **verified**.

Here we use an independent source: **revenues** in Compustat Global. Both should report the group's net revenues in millions of the reporting currency.

### Chunk 5.1 · Compustat Global

```{r chunk_5_1}
## Read Compustat Global (gvkey as text, look at all rows before guessing types)
cs_g <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat_global_2023_2025.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(gvkey = "c"), guess_max = Inf)

## Key check: one row per isin + fyear?
cs_g |> count(isin, fyear) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()

## Same story as in Compustat North America: INDL and FS formats ...
cs_g <- cs_g |> filter(indfmt == "INDL")

## ... and firms that changed their fiscal year-end (two datadates per fyear)
cs_g <- cs_g |>
  group_by(isin, fyear) |>
  slice_max(datadate, n = 1) |>      # keep the later datadate (same rule as Chunk 3.3c)
  ungroup()
cs_g |> count(isin, fyear) |> filter(n > 1) |> nrow()   # 0 = key unique now
```

### Chunk 5.2 · Merge by ISIN and year

```{r chunk_5_2}
## SRN revenues, one row per firm-year, with currency added
srn_cur <- srn_raw |> filter(field_slug == "currency") |>
  transmute(isin, year, srn_currency = value)
srn_rev <- srn_raw |> filter(field_slug == "revenues", !is.na(isin)) |>
  transmute(isin, year, company_name, unit, source,
            srn_revenue = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |>
  left_join(srn_cur, by = c("isin", "year"))

## Who extracted the revenue value: human or AI?
srn_rev |> count(source)

## Merge with Compustat Global by ISIN and year
merged <- srn_rev |>
  inner_join(cs_g |> select(isin, fyear, conm, curcd, revt),
             by = c("isin", "year" = "fyear"))
nrow(srn_rev); nrow(merged)          # before / after (after must not be larger!)

## Which SRN firm-years found no partner in Compustat Global?
no_partner <- srn_rev |> anti_join(cs_g, by = c("isin", "year" = "fyear"))
nrow(no_partner)
head(no_partner)

## Banks and insurers are only in the FS format — our INDL filter removed them
cs_g_fs <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat_global_2023_2025.csv"),
                    col_types = cols(gvkey = "c"), guess_max = Inf) |>
  filter(indfmt == "FS")
no_partner |> semi_join(cs_g_fs, by = c("isin", "year" = "fyear")) |> nrow()   # lost only because of INDL
```

### Chunk 5.3 · Do the numbers agree?

```{r chunk_5_3}
## Compare only where both values exist and the currency is the same
cmp <- merged |>
  filter(!is.na(srn_revenue), !is.na(revt), revt > 0) |>
  mutate(ratio = srn_revenue / revt)              # 1 = perfect agreement
cmp |> count(same_currency = srn_currency == curcd)
cmp_same <- cmp |> filter(srn_currency == curcd)

## Share that agrees within 2% (slide: 88% overall, AI 87%, human 90%)
cmp_same |>
  group_by(source) |>
  summarise(share_2pct = mean(abs(ratio - 1) <= 0.02), n = n())

## Typical patterns of disagreement
cmp_same |>
  mutate(pattern = case_when(
    abs(ratio - 1) <= 0.02        ~ "agree (within 2%)",
    between(ratio, 900, 1100)     ~ "SRN about 1,000x larger (units: thousands?)",
    between(ratio, 0.0009, 0.0011) ~ "SRN about 1,000x smaller (units)",
    TRUE                          ~ "other: year, definition or extraction error?")) |>
  count(pattern)

## The biggest disagreements — look them up in the report!
cmp_same |>
  arrange(desc(abs(log(ratio)))) |>               # largest deviation in either direction
  select(company_name, isin, year, source, unit, srn_revenue, revt, ratio) |>
  head(10)
```

**Task C:** Pick one firm with a large disagreement. Typical reasons: units (thousands vs. millions), currency, a different revenue definition, the wrong year — or an extraction error. Which is it? Who is right: SRN or Compustat?
```{r task_C}
## Where did SRN get Ontex's 2025 revenue from?
srn_raw |>
  filter(isin == "BE0974276082", year == 2025, field_slug == "revenues") |>
  select(company_name, value, unit, source, source_document_id, page_reference)
```
Answer C: Ontex 2025. SRN (AI-extracted): 111.2 m EUR, Compustat: 1,761.6 m EUR (ratio 0.06).
Not units, currency or year. SRN's page 125 shows the revenue of the discontinued operations
(Brazil and Turkey, sold in 2025), not group revenue. Group revenue is 1,761.6 m (p. 117),
exactly as in Compustat. Compustat is right: an AI extraction error (right label, wrong table).

# Part 6 · Bug hunt: an AI-written merge script

An **assertion** is a check that stops your code when something is not as expected:

```{r chunk_6_0, error=TRUE}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
stopifnot(length(x) == 3)        # OK: nothing happens
stopifnot(all(x > 1))            # stops with an error message
```

Three assertions you can use in almost every merge:

-   the key is unique: `stopifnot(!any(duplicated(data[c("gvkey", "fyear")])))`
-   no rows were added by a join: `stopifnot(nrow(after) == nrow(before))`
-   identifiers look right: `stopifnot(all(nchar(data$gvkey) == 6))`

The script below was written by an AI for the prompt *"Merge Compustat with CRSP returns and the SRN revenues. Count the firms in the final sample."* It runs — mostly. **Find the bugs** (10 min by hand, then 10 min with an AI tool of your choice — code only, never the data).

### Chunk 6.1 · The AI-generated script

```{r chunk_6_1, error=TRUE}
## ---- AI-generated script ----

## (a) Compustat: read the data
comp <- read.csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"))
comp <- comp |> filter(!is.na(fyear))

## (b) Link Compustat to CRSP
comp_crsp <- comp |>
  mutate(gvkey = as.character(gvkey)) |>
  left_join(link, by = "gvkey", relationship = "many-to-many")

## (c) Number of firms with a CRSP link
cat("Firms with CRSP link:", n_distinct(comp_crsp$gvkey), "\n")

## (d) Average monthly return per firm
avg_ret <- msf_raw |>
  group_by(permno) |>
  summarise(mean_ret = mean(mthret))
cat("Firms with returns:", sum(!is.na(avg_ret$mean_ret)), "\n")

## (e) SRN revenues in wide format
srn_rev_wide <- srn_raw |>
  filter(field_slug %in% c("revenues", "employees_total")) |>
  select(company_name, year, field_slug, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = field_slug, values_from = value)

## (f) Revenue per employee
srn_rev_wide <- srn_rev_wide |>
  mutate(rev_per_emp = as.numeric(revenues) / as.numeric(employees_total))
summary(srn_rev_wide$rev_per_emp)
```

### Chunk 6.2 · Solution: bugs and fixes

Write your corrected version below. Add an assertion after every fix.

```{r chunk_6_2}
## (a) Read Compustat safely: gvkey as text, one format, one row per firm-year
comp <- read_csv(here("data", "compustat.csv"), col_types = cols(gvkey = "c"), guess_max = Inf) |>
  filter(!is.na(fyear), indfmt == "INDL") |>
  group_by(gvkey, fyear) |> slice_max(datadate, n = 1) |> ungroup()
stopifnot(all(nchar(comp$gvkey) == 6))                          # IDs keep leading zeros
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(comp[c("gvkey", "fyear")])))          # key unique

## (b) Link with the date condition, inner join = only firm-years WITH a valid link
comp_crsp <- comp |>
  inner_join(link, by = join_by(gvkey, between(datadate, linkdt, linkenddt)))
stopifnot(nrow(comp_crsp) <= nrow(comp))                        # no rows added (no fan-out)
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(comp_crsp[c("gvkey", "fyear")])))     # still one row per firm-year

## (c) Firms with a CRSP link
cat("Firms with CRSP link:", n_distinct(comp_crsp$gvkey), "\n")

## (d) Average monthly return per firm: cleaned file, missing months ignored
avg_ret <- msf_clean |>
  group_by(permno) |>
  summarise(mean_ret = mean(mthret, na.rm = TRUE))
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(avg_ret$permno)))                     # one row per permno
cat("Firms with returns:", sum(!is.na(avg_ret$mean_ret)), "\n")

## (e) SRN in wide format: real key (company_id), numbers instead of text
srn_rev_wide <- srn_raw |>
  filter(field_slug %in% c("revenues", "employees_total", "currency")) |>
  select(company_id, year, field_slug, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = field_slug, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(revenues        = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(revenues)),          # NOT_FOUND -> NA (on purpose)
         employees_total = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(employees_total)))
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(srn_rev_wide[c("company_id", "year")])))

## (f) Revenue per employee: in thousands per employee, compared only within one currency
srn_rev_wide <- srn_rev_wide |>
  mutate(rev_per_emp_k = revenues * 1000 / employees_total)    # millions -> thousands per employee
srn_rev_wide |>
  group_by(currency) |>
  summarise(median_k = median(rev_per_emp_k, na.rm = TRUE), n = n())
```
